Understanding cancer staging

Stage describes how large a cancer is and how far it has spread. It helps your team plan treatment, estimate outlook and find clinical trials that fit.

The TNM system

Most solid tumors are staged with three letters, each followed by a number:

  • T — TumorThe size of the main (primary) tumor and how far it has grown into nearby tissue.
  • N — NodesWhether cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes. N0 means no.
  • M — MetastasisWhether cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. M0 means no; M1 means yes.

Stages 0 to IV

  • Stage 0 — abnormal cells that have not spread into nearby tissue (carcinoma in situ).
  • Stages I, II and III — cancer is present; higher numbers usually mean a larger tumor or more spread into nearby tissues or lymph nodes.
  • Stage IV — cancer has spread to distant parts of the body.

The same TNM letters can mean different stages in different cancers, so compare only within your own cancer type.

Blood cancers are different

  • Lymphomas use their own staging (based on which lymph node areas and organs are involved).
  • Myeloma uses a system based largely on blood tests and genetic features of the myeloma cells.
  • Most leukemias are not given a stage; type, genetic features and blood counts guide treatment instead.

Good to know

  • The stage given at diagnosis stays the same, even if the cancer later grows or comes back. New information is added to it, for example “stage II, now recurrent.”
  • Stage and grade are different: grade describes how the cells look under the microscope. See your pathology report.
  • Stage is about the cancer, not about you. Many people with advanced cancer live well for years with modern treatment. Ask what your stage means for your own plan.
